title: Password Policy
story: A startup's database was breached because users registered with '123' as their password. The system accepted any string, no matter how weak. An invariant type would have enforced policy at the data layer itself.
why: Security policies encoded as type invariants are impossible to bypass — the policy lives in the type, not in scattered validation code.
analogy: A Password type is like a locked safe — only valid combinations can be placed inside. Once it's in, you can operate on it (count strength) without checking if it's actually a password.
try_it: Add real character-class detection to `strength`: check for uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and special characters (!@#$%). Each gives +1 to the score. The invariant handles minimum length — your code handles everything else.
tips: Security policies as invariants make audits trivial — grep for 'type.*invariant' and you've found every enforced constraint
`mask` is a read-only method that never exposes the plaintext — the borrow checker guarantees `&self` doesn't mutate
Strength scoring is additive — no penalty for failure because the invariant already rejected weak passwords at construction
common_mistakes: Hardcoding password policy rules in multiple functions — when policy changes, you'll miss one
Exposing `self.value` directly — always use methods like `mask()` and `strength()` that control what's revealed
Forgetting that `mask` must handle arbitrary-length passwords — the invariant says >= 8, but it could be 100 characters
